title: Rivers and seas
hook: rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower (Tao Te Ching 66)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard chapter: two readings of the word simple. Your line was read it twice. What did you read a second time before answering? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

A good guide on a mountain trail walks in front, and somehow nobody feels dragged. A good host fills the whole evening, and nobody feels crowded. A good coach is clearly in charge, and the players still feel like it's their game. Chapter sixty-one, a few days back, used a low river to describe a great country. Chapter sixty-six brings the water back, this time to describe one person who leads. And it says the secret of those guides and hosts is the same as the secret of the sea. Today, rivers and seas.
screen: `IN FRONT, BUT NOBODY DRAGGED.` → `THE WATER COMES BACK.` → `THE SECRET OF THE SEA.`

segments.voice: First, kings of the valleys. In James Legge's translation, rivers and seas receive the tribute of all the valley streams because of "their skill in being lower than they." They don't conquer the streams. They don't call them. They're simply lower, and so everything comes to them. The chapter calls that being king. Second, words below, steps behind. The sage, the chapter says, who wants to be above the people, puts his words below them. Wanting to lead them, he puts himself behind them. That's an odd recipe for leadership. Speak as if from underneath. Walk at the back. Third, nobody feels the weight. When such a person is above, the chapter says, the people don't feel any burden. When such a person is in front, they don't feel any harm. And so the whole world is glad to push this person forward, and doesn't tire of it. Leadership, in this picture, isn't something you grab. It's something others keep handing you, because you're easy to carry. Fourth, no contest. The chapter ends on a line the Tao Te Ching also uses in chapter twenty-two: because this person doesn't compete, nobody in the world can compete with them. Around us, this looks like the manager who asks before she tells, the older sibling who lets the younger one go first, the expert who explains without making anyone feel slow. They lie lower, and everything finds its way to them.
screen: `KINGS OF THE VALLEYS.` · `WORDS BELOW, STEPS BEHIND.` · `NOBODY FEELS THE WEIGHT.` · then, large: `NO CONTEST, NO RIVAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lower yourself once. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle low in your belly. Bring to mind one place where you're ahead of someone. You're older, or more senior, or simply know more about the thing. Picture a moment there that's coming soon. Now try the chapter's recipe on it. Words below: what would you ask, instead of announce? Steps behind: where could you let them go first? Don't plan a speech. Find one small way to lie a little lower, and hold it gently. The bell holds the time.
Rivers and seas. In chapter sixty-six, they're king of the valley streams because they lie lower. Today's word.
Your line: they lie lower. Once today, in a place where you're ahead, put your words below someone else's: ask before you tell. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-six as a picture of servant leadership: the one who leads speaks humbly, stays behind, and does not compete for the front.

fork.setup: you want to lead a group. chapter sixty-six describes how the sage ends up in front. how?
options: put words below them and self behind.
wait until someone names you leader.
fork.reveal: the sage who wants to be above the people puts his words below them, and to lead them, puts himself behind them.

original.note: Chinese: good at being low, the skill of rivers and seas in chapter sixty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: rivers and seas sounds like a geography lesson.
what it means: the one who lies lowest becomes the place everything flows to, and leads without weighing on anyone.
what a scholar hears: the chapter's closing line, that no one can compete with one who doesn't compete, also appears in chapter twenty-two.

notes: Check the Legge 1891 quotation of chapter 66 ('their skill in being lower than they') word for word.
Trapdoor and teach say the non-contending line also appears in chapter 22 (夫唯不爭，故天下莫能與之爭); confirm.
The index hook says 'a hundred valleys'; the script says 'all the valley streams' to avoid stating a number.
The guide, host, coach, manager and sibling images are the writer's illustrations.
Original 善下 (shàn xià) rendered approximately; confirm.
